bank: Bank of England · Monetary Authority of Singapore · Bank of Thailand
title: Who bears the risk when separate currency systems settle one FX trade?
summary: Project Meridian FX APAC found that a common operator could co-ordinate payment-versus-payment across three differently designed central bank test systems. Its policy report asks what a bank would need to know before relying on that mechanism to discharge a live FX obligation. The pivotal issue is what the operator actually does. Permission to send instructions, temporary control over the money being delivered, and responsibility for calculating net settlement obligations each create a different dependency. A successful test establishes that currencies can be linked operationally. The applicable legal frameworks must still determine what happens to each leg during a dispute, insolvency or outage.

The starting model leaves funds with the participants. The synchronisation operator matches their instructions, arranges for money to be set aside, monitors readiness and tells the underlying infrastructures when settlement can proceed. In that model it need not run either ledger or maintain settlement accounts. Yet its decision to proceed, retry or release reservations can directly determine whether participants get paid on time. Section 2 explains why even a non-custodial operator can become critical to domestic systems. The scale of the service and the extent of reliance on it would matter for oversight alongside its formal status.

The experiment also illustrates how an implementation choice changes the legal question. In the Singapore test environment, a dedicated escrow account replicated a reservation facility. Temporary control over funds raises questions about safeguarding, access in insolvency and responsibility for liquidity that do not arise in the same form when funds stay earmarked in a participant’s account. In the multilateral exercise, the operator calculated participants’ net positions. That brings its role closer to clearing. Neither function is intrinsic to synchronisation. System-specific adaptations can expand access while changing which institution must answer for funds or for the calculation of obligations.

Section 4 applies five policy lenses to existing arrangements. Australia’s batch administrator arrangements illustrate how an operator could obtain assured access to settlement infrastructure without receiving an account in central bank money. Swift illustrates how a lead overseer can co-ordinate authorities, although a synchronisation operator exercises more influence over execution than a messaging provider. CLS achieves a legally recognised FX settlement outcome on a shared ledger. Here, separate ledgers and domestic rules would have to produce a jointly understood point of irrevocability. For governance, the international Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures and the Global Layer One toolkit offer starting points for assigning responsibility among the operator, participants and domestic authorities. Common financial message formats could improve reconciliation across the systems, but the authorities would still have to establish who may share which data, on what legal basis and for how long.

The report organises the remaining decisions by who can make them. Domestic authorities can set access conditions, test an operator’s fitness and assess operating-hour arrangements. Cross-border agreement is needed where decisions in one system determine liability or the treatment of a failed leg elsewhere. International principles could support consistency while accommodating different domestic capabilities. Section 5 also calls attention to opening hours and the life of an earmark. A bank waiting for a second system to reopen may have its funds tied up even if the settlement design ultimately protects the amount due. For a treasury desk, the contract governing that interval is as consequential as the software’s ability to finish the trade.

questions.question: When can each counterparty treat its obligation as legally discharged?
questions.detail: The experiment establishes a workflow commitment point. The report leaves national insolvency treatment and cross-border finality open. Both matter for principal exposure if a counterparty or operator enters resolution between the first and last posting. Obtain the domestic settlement rulebooks and legal opinions addressing that interval in a proposed live service. Look for recognition of earmarks, irrevocability and the remedies that survive insolvency in each participating jurisdiction.

questions.question: Who controls escrowed funds if the operator fails?
questions.detail: The policy report identifies custody and safeguarding concerns in the test arrangement, while leaving the rights of participants under a live contract unresolved. A participant deciding how much liquidity to place there needs evidence on segregation, access and the time required to recover the balance. Review the proposed custody agreement, the account-holding institution’s rules and applicable insolvency protections, then compare them with an otherwise identical trade using a domestic earmark.

questions.question: What happens to a bank’s liquidity when one national settlement day ends first?
questions.detail: Domestic authorities could set their own hours and reservation policies, but the paper supplies no live estimates of the resulting cash requirement. A treasury desk choosing an intraday liquidity buffer would want the distribution of reservation times, especially around cut-offs and disruptions. Ask participating operators for operating calendars, expiry policies and scenario tests of overnight holds. Compare those results with settlement during a shorter common window.

limitation: The policy paper describes test systems and leaves live rules, enforceability and liability for future decisions. It reports no realised FX settlement losses or market-price effects.
